blocks.text: ISABELA CITY, BASILAN, Philippines — For decades, the dominant public perception among many Filipinos of the seafaring Sama Badjau in urban centers has been reduced to a painful stereotype: outstretched palms on city streets, begging for “limos” (alms). But in coastal Barangay Tampalan, where roughly 70 percent of residents belong to the Sama Badjau ethnic group (commonly referred to as Badjaos), a peaceful revolution is dismantling that narrative—not through “ayuda” (dole-outs) but through the rhythmic, intricate interlacing of dried pandan leaves.
